name: Binary Fuse Filter demo (FastFilter/FilterPassword)
workload: Build & query benchmark over 10M password-hash-derived 64-bit keys (HaveIBeenPwned SHA1 list) comparing a binaryfuse8 filter vs a bloom12 filter built and queried with the project's build_filter/query_filter CLI tools.
claimed_speedup: Construction: 0.420s vs 0.613s (~1.46x faster). Serialized size: 11,272,228 vs 15,000,024 bytes (~1.33x smaller). Single-query wall time: 241µs vs 344µs, i.e. ~4,149 vs ~2,907 expected queries/sec (~1.43x, from one-off timings, not averaged).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 11 on Ubuntu 22.04 per CI badge; no explicit optimization flags shown for the reported run
tradeoffs: Filter is immutable (build-once, no add/remove); construction needs ~64 bytes/entry RAM even though the finished filter uses ~1 byte/entry; project explicitly a demonstration, not the library to depend on (library is FastFilter/xor_singleheader).
caveats: Single-run wall-clock numbers copied from example README commands, not repeated/averaged; CPU model not stated; no LICENSE file found in the repo.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "binary fuse filter"

name: efuse_filter (Erlang NIF, Binary Fuse Filter)
workload: Benchee suite (mpope9/exor_bechmark) builds filters of 1k/100k/1M/10M elements and times 10,000 reads from each, comparing efuse_filter's fuse8 against three Erlang/Elixir Bloom filter libraries (Bloomex, Blex, erbloom).
claimed_speedup: fuse8 8 1M: 1.42ms avg (705.7 ips) vs Bloomex 1M 8.87ms (6.7x slower), Blex 1M 13.17ms (9.9x slower), erbloom 1M 4.01ms (2.8x slower). fuse8 8 10M: 1.54ms avg (648.4 ips) vs Bloomex 10M 15.24ms (11.5x slower), Blex 10M 18.47ms (13.9x slower), erbloom 10M 3.90ms (2.95x slower). (numbers from the shootout's Benchee output)
compiler_and_flags: Elixir 1.12.2, Erlang/OTP 24.0.5; underlying Rust NIF compiler/opt flags not stated
hardware: Intel Core i5-7267U CPU @ 3.10GHz, 4 cores, 8GB RAM, macOS (per repo's own Benchee output)
tradeoffs: Filters are immutable once finalized; incremental build path uses Erlang `sets` and has a higher memory footprint than the batch API; NIF-based (Rust), so requires native compilation.
caveats: Benchmark suite (exor_bechmark) was written by the same author as efuse_filter/exor_filter, not an independent third party; run on a laptop, which the benchmark repo itself flags as 'not a production environment'; Rust NIF build flags not documented, so capped below A/B despite detailed CPU/software-version reporting. This is a shootout repo; efuse_filter is reported here as the identified winner among fuse/xor variants for large N.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "binary fuse filter" -> mpope9/efuse_filter -> linked mpope9/exor_bechmark

name: exor_filter (Erlang NIF, Xor Filter)
workload: Same Benchee shootout (mpope9/exor_bechmark) as efuse_filter above: filters of 1k/100k/1M/10M elements, 10,000 reads each, comparing exor_filter's xor8/xor16 against Bloomex, Blex, and erbloom.
claimed_speedup: xor8 8 1M: 1.55ms avg (645.2 ips) vs Bloomex 1M 8.87ms (5.7x slower), Blex 1M 13.17ms (8.5x slower), erbloom 1M 4.01ms (2.6x slower). xor16 10M: 1.77ms avg (565.4 ips) vs Bloomex 10M 15.24ms (8.6x slower), Blex 10M 18.47ms (10.4x slower), erbloom 10M 3.90ms (2.2x slower).
compiler_and_flags: Elixir 1.12.2, Erlang/OTP 24.0.5; underlying Rust NIF compiler/opt flags not stated
hardware: Intel Core i5-7267U CPU @ 3.10GHz, 4 cores, 8GB RAM, macOS (per repo's own Benchee output)
tradeoffs: Filters are immutable once finalized; large (>10K element) initialization uses dirty NIFs and needs correct VM scheduler config; NIF-based (Rust), needs native compilation.
caveats: Same non-independent benchmark author/caveats as efuse_filter entry above; xor8/xor16 are themselves in the 'xor filter' baseline family, but the qualifying comparison here is against Bloom filter libraries (Bloomex/Blex/erbloom), which is what is being reported.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos topic:xor-filter -> mpope9/exor_filter -> linked mpope9/exor_bechmark

name: xor-filter (Java, komiya-atsushi)
workload: Query throughput (queries/ms) and serialization size for Long and String keys, comparing this Xor Filter (8-bit, 16-bit) against Guava Bloom filters at fpp=0.389% and fpp=0.002%.
claimed_speedup: Long keys: 17,458 q/ms (xor8) vs 8,879 q/ms (bloom fpp=0.389%), ~1.97x. String keys: 7,122 q/ms (xor8) vs 5,318 q/ms (bloom fpp=0.389%), ~1.34x. Serialization: 123,042 bytes / 9.843 bits-per-entry (xor8) vs 144,390 bytes / 11.551 bits-per-entry (bloom fpp=0.389%), ~1.17x smaller.
tradeoffs: Immutable filter (build once); needs Guava for the Funnels API; example dependency snippet references a defunct Bintray repo (library itself is on Maven Central).
caveats: No JVM version, warm-up/iteration count, or CPU model documented for the benchmark table; project unmaintained since 2020.

name: BinaryFuseFilter (.NET)
workload: BenchmarkDotNet run on .NET 10 x64: mixed hit/miss query-latency and construction-time ratios over 1,000,000 pre-hashed 64-bit keys, comparing BinaryFuse8Filter against BloomFilter.NetCore (same 0.39% FPP) and XORFilterDotNet.
claimed_speedup: Query: BloomFilter.NetCore time ratio 20.76 vs BinaryFuse8Filter's 1.00 (BloomFilter.NetCore ~20.76x slower). Construction: BloomFilter.NetCore ratio 2.32 (86x more allocation) vs 1.00 for BinaryFuse8Filter. Also beats XORFilterDotNet (8.68x slower query; 58.6x slower / 366x more allocation to construct).
compiler_and_flags: .NET 10, Release configuration, BenchmarkDotNet (`dotnet run -c Release --project src/BinaryFuseFilter.Benchmarks`)
tradeoffs: Filter is immutable after construction (no add/remove); pure managed C#, no native dependencies.
caveats: Very new, single-author repo (1 star); CPU model not stated so capped below A/B; the 20x query-speed ratio may partly reflect BloomFilter.NetCore's implementation rather than a fundamental limit of Bloom filters in general.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "binary fuse filter"

name: Bloomsday (blocked/split-block Bloom filter, Rust)
baseline: Bloom filter (sbbf-rs Split Block Bloom Filter crate)
workload: Criterion benchmark of positive and negative membership lookups on a 1,000,000-item filter built for a 0.01 false-positive rate, comparing this auto-vectorized blocked Bloom filter against the sbbf-rs crate (benches/comparison.rs wraps sbbf-rs's FilterFn directly).
claimed_speedup: Negative lookup: ~1.17µs (bloomsday) vs ~2.81µs (sbbf-rs), ~2.4x. Positive lookup: ~1.26µs (bloomsday) vs ~2.93µs (sbbf-rs), ~2.3x.
compiler_and_flags: Rust + Criterion; README states results require `-C target-feature=+avx2` or `target-cpu=native` to let LLVM auto-vectorize, but does not confirm these flags were used for the published numbers
license: MIT (declared in Cargo.toml; no separate LICENSE file detected by GitHub)
tradeoffs: 100% safe Rust (no unsafe blocks); relies on compiler auto-vectorization instead of explicit SIMD intrinsics, so performance is sensitive to build flags; single-author, very new project.
caveats: Beats a specific Rust Split-Block-Bloom-Filter crate (sbbf-rs), not a canonical/hand-optimized C/C++ Bloom filter; no CPU model stated; whether the required autovectorization flags were actually used for the published numbers is unconfirmed.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "blocked bloom filter"

name: pleat (Pleated Ribbon Filter, Rust)
workload: Own Criterion benchmarks (cargo bench --bench construct/query/serde) of ribbon-filter construction throughput (pleated vs arrival-order vs 8-thread parallel) and query latency at 1M and 10M 64-bit keys; README states ribbon filters use ~7.6 bits/key at ~0.8% FPR, 'well under a Bloom filter's memory for the same accuracy'.
claimed_speedup: Memory: ~7.6 bits/key at 0.8% FPR, described as well under Bloom filter memory for equal accuracy (qualitative, no Bloom bits/key number given on the same page). Construction: pleated build is ~2.3x faster than the crate's own arrival-order build once the table exceeds L3 cache (26.0ns/key vs 60.4ns/key at 10M keys) -- this ratio is against the crate's own baseline construction order, not against a Bloom filter implementation.
license: MIT OR Apache-2.0 (GitHub license detector reports MIT)
tradeoffs: Immutable filter (build-once); keys must be pre-hashed to u64; this release implements homogeneous ribbon (w=64) plus a StdRibbon w=128 variant; construction still needs the full banding table in memory like other ribbon filters.
caveats: The direct 'faster/smaller than Bloom' claims are qualitative statements in the README, not numbers measured against an actual Bloom filter implementation on the same benchmark page; the only head-to-head numeric comparison on the page is pleated vs the crate's own arrival-order construction. Very new project (1 star).

name: compressed_map ApproxSet (frayed ribbon filter)
workload: Author's own qualitative comparison (README) of ApproxSet, a frayed-ribbon-filter-based approximate set, against Bloom filters; no specific dataset size or key type given.
claimed_speedup: "Compared to Bloom filters, ApproxSets take several times longer (and several times more memory) to construct; are faster to query; and take about 30% less space." (verbatim). Only the ~30% space figure is a concrete number; query/construction-speed differences are stated only qualitatively.
tradeoffs: Construction is explicitly slower and more memory-hungry than a Bloom filter for the same set; author labels the whole library 'research-grade... don't deploy it in production'; C FFI incomplete; depends on a pre-release bincode version.
caveats: No benchmark numbers, dataset, or methodology for the query-speed or construction-time claims -- only the space-saving figure is numeric; no commits since November 2022.

name: Vector Quotient Filter (VQF)
workload: SIGMOD 2021 paper's insert/lookup/delete throughput measurements across load factors for a SIMD (AVX-512/AVX2) Robin-Hood-hashed quotient filter, including a thread-safe concurrent-insert variant.
claimed_speedup: 2x faster inserts than the Morton filter (a cuckoo-filter variant, described in the paper as state-of-the-art for inserts); lookup and deletion performance similar to the cuckoo filter (described as fastest for queries/deletes); concurrent insert throughput scales 3x with 4 threads vs 1 thread; minimal performance decline at high load factors vs quotient, cuckoo, and Morton filters.
tradeoffs: Depends on libssl; requires AVX-512 (or AVX2 fallback) instructions; more complex build than a plain Bloom or cuckoo filter.
caveats: Headline 2x speed claim is against the Morton filter, not directly Bloom/cuckoo/xor; vs cuckoo filter itself the paper claims only parity ('similar lookup and deletion performance'), not a win. CPU model, compiler, and flags for the paper's measurements were not accessible this session -- dl.acm.org returned HTTP 403 and the VMware research PDF host returned a server error; the abstract text used here was confirmed via a GitHub-hosted paper-index mirror (raw.githubusercontent.com), not the full paper.
